blog.intro: Trends, buzzwords and tech explained in plain language — from agentic AI to digital twins — for business owners and teams across every industry.

items.title: What is agentic AI? AI agents explained for business
items.seoTitle: What Is Agentic AI? AI Agents Explained for South African Businesses
items.description: Agentic AI is the shift from chatbots that answer to AI agents that act. What agents are, how they work, where they help in finance, retail, logistics and healthcare — and the guardrails they need.
items.imageAlt: A friendly AI agent orchestrating documents, a calendar, a checklist and a settings gear
takeaways: A chatbot answers questions; an AI agent plans steps and uses tools to complete a task.
Agents work best on repeatable, well-defined jobs with clear rules and data.
Keep a human approval step for anything involving money, customers or personal information.
Under POPIA, personal information handled by an agent still needs a lawful reason, protection and limited access.

p: For the past few years most people met AI as a chat window: you ask, it answers. Agentic AI is the next step. Instead of only replying, an AI agent is given a goal and a set of tools, then plans and carries out the steps needed to reach it — checking its own progress along the way.
That shift from talking to doing is why “agentic” has become one of the biggest buzzwords in technology. Here’s what it actually means in practice.

head: Spec
In plain terms
rows: AI that pursues a goal by planning steps and taking actions, not just replying
A language model, instructions, tools it may use, memory and guardrails
Email, calendars, spreadsheets, CRMs, databases and internal systems
Repeatable multi-step work: triage, follow-ups, reconciliation, reporting
Wrong actions, data leakage, runaway costs and unclear accountability
Set the goal and rules, approve key actions, review the results

list: Goal — a clear instruction, such as “chase every invoice that is more than 30 days overdue”.
Planning — the model breaks the goal into steps and decides which tool to use for each one.
Tools — connections to real systems: reading a spreadsheet, drafting an email, updating a record.
Memory — notes about what has been done, so the agent doesn’t repeat itself.
Guardrails — limits on what it may do on its own, and when it must stop and ask a person.
Finance — matching payments to invoices, flagging anomalies and preparing reports for review.
Retail and ecommerce — answering order queries, updating stock records and drafting product descriptions.
Logistics — monitoring deliveries, spotting delays and notifying customers.
Healthcare administration — booking, reminders and summarising forms, with clinicians making decisions.
Professional services — gathering information for proposals and keeping CRMs up to date.

p: Agents can be confidently wrong, and an agent that acts on a mistake does more damage than a chatbot that only says something odd. Common problems are vague goals, tools with too much access, no record of what the agent did and no human checkpoint before irreversible actions.

list: Give each agent the smallest set of permissions it needs.
Require approval before payments, deletions or messages to customers.
Log every action so you can see what happened and why.
Set spending and usage limits on the AI services behind it.
Treat personal information carefully — POPIA still applies when software does the processing.

p: Pick one repetitive, well-documented task with a clear definition of “done”. Run the agent alongside a person first, measure the results and only then let it act on its own within firm limits. Our Workflow Automation and AI Assistants services are built around exactly this kind of careful, step-by-step adoption.

items.title: What is MCP? The Model Context Protocol explained
items.seoTitle: What Is MCP (Model Context Protocol)? A Plain-English Guide
items.description: MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. What it is, how it works, why it matters and what to check before you connect anything.
items.imageAlt: A universal connector hub with cables plugging in from a database, documents, a calendar and a chat bubble
takeaways: MCP is an open standard that lets AI applications connect to tools and data in one consistent way.
It is often described as “USB-C for AI”: build a connection once, use it with many AI apps.
An MCP server exposes tools, data and prompt templates; an AI app connects to it as a client.
Every connection is access to your systems — permissions, logging and trusted sources matter.

p: An AI assistant is only as useful as the information and tools it can reach. Until recently, every connection — to your calendar, your database, your documents — had to be custom-built for each AI product. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that changes that.

head: Spec
In plain terms
rows: Open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data
By Anthropic in late 2024, since adopted across major AI platforms and developer tools
Client–server: AI apps are clients; MCP servers expose capabilities
Fewer one-off integrations and easier switching between AI providers

p: Imagine five AI tools and ten business systems. Without a standard, that could mean fifty separate integrations. With MCP, each system is wrapped once as an MCP server, and any AI application that supports MCP can use it. That is why it is often compared to USB-C: one plug shape for many devices.

list: MCP server — a small service that sits in front of a system (a database, a file store, a ticketing tool) and describes what it can do.
MCP client — the AI application, such as an assistant or a coding tool, that discovers those capabilities and uses them.
Tools — actions the AI may take, like “create a ticket” or “look up an order”.
Resources — data the AI may read, like documents or records.
Prompts — reusable instructions that help the AI use the server well.
Internal assistants that can look up policies, orders or stock levels.
Developer tools that read code, run tests and open issues.
Customer support assistants that check order status in real systems.
Agents that move information between tools as part of a workflow.

sections.h: What to check before connecting anything
list: Use servers from sources you trust, or build your own.
Give each server read-only access unless writing is genuinely needed.
Keep credentials out of prompts and rotate them regularly.
Log tool calls so you can audit what the AI did.
Decide which actions need a person to approve them first.

p: MCP doesn’t make AI smarter — it makes it better connected. For businesses, that means AI assistants that work with your real information, built with integrations that are easier to maintain and less tied to a single provider.

items.title: RAG explained: how AI answers from your own documents
items.seoTitle: RAG Explained: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Businesses
items.description: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets AI answer questions from your own documents instead of guessing. How it works, embeddings and vector search in plain terms, where it is used and how to keep it accurate.
items.imageAlt: A filing drawer of documents with a magnifying lens lifting pages into a glowing speech bubble
takeaways: RAG finds the most relevant passages in your documents and gives them to the AI before it answers.
It reduces made-up answers and lets the AI quote and link its sources.
Answer quality depends on document quality: outdated or messy files produce poor answers.
Access rules matter — people should only get answers from documents they are allowed to see.

p: Large language models are trained on huge amounts of public text, but they don’t know your price list, your HR policy or last month’s product update. Ask them anyway and they may produce a fluent, confident guess. Retrieval-augmented generation — RAG — fixes this by giving the model the right information at the moment it answers.

head: Spec
In plain terms
rows: Retrieves relevant information first, then generates an answer grounded in it
Your documents, an embedding model, a vector index and a language model
Numbers that capture meaning, so similar ideas can be found even with different words
Policies, product manuals, contracts, FAQs, knowledge bases
Stale content, missing access controls and answers without citations

list: Prepare — documents are split into small passages.
Embed — each passage is converted into an embedding: a list of numbers representing its meaning.
Index — the embeddings are stored in a vector index so they can be searched by meaning.
Retrieve — when someone asks a question, the most relevant passages are found.
Generate — the model writes an answer using those passages, ideally citing them.

p: Traditional search matches words. Vector search matches ideas, so a question about “annual leave” can find a policy that only says “vacation days”. Many systems combine both approaches for the best results.

sections.h: Where it is used across industries
list: Banking and insurance — answering staff questions from long policy and product documents.
Legal — finding relevant clauses across contracts.
Healthcare — helping staff find procedures and administrative guidance.
Manufacturing and mining — searching manuals, maintenance logs and safety procedures.
Customer support — answering from help articles and order information.
Remove outdated documents and keep one current version of each.
Show the sources behind every answer so people can check them.
Respect permissions so confidential files never reach the wrong person.
Test with real questions and review the answers that go wrong.
Tell the assistant to say “I don’t know” when the documents don’t cover a question.

p: If your team spends time hunting through documents or answering the same questions repeatedly, RAG is often the most practical first AI project. Our AI Assistants service scopes the sources, permissions and testing so answers stay grounded in your information.

items.title: Vibe coding explained: what it is, where it works and where it breaks
items.seoTitle: Vibe Coding Explained: Benefits, Risks and When to Get Help
items.description: Vibe coding means building software by describing what you want to an AI. What it is, the tools behind it, where it shines for prototypes — and the security, data and maintenance problems to fix before launch.
items.imageAlt: A laptop with code blocks rising like bricks, with one cracked brick tilting off the stack
takeaways: Vibe coding is building software by describing it in plain language and letting AI write the code.
It is excellent for prototypes, internal tools and testing ideas quickly.
Generated apps often hide problems: weak security, exposed keys, poor data handling and no tests.
Before real customers or real data, have the code reviewed, secured and made maintainable.

p: “Vibe coding” went from a throwaway phrase to a global trend remarkably quickly. The idea is simple: describe the app you want, let an AI generate the code, try it, describe what to change and repeat. Many people have built working prototypes in an afternoon this way.

head: Spec
In plain terms
rows: Creating software by prompting an AI and iterating on the results, often without reading much of the code
By AI researcher Andrej Karpathy in early 2025
AI app builders and AI coding assistants inside code editors
Prototypes, demos, internal tools and early product experiments
Authentication, access rules, secrets management, error handling, tests
Security review, data protection, performance checks and documentation

list: Speed — an idea can become a clickable prototype in hours.
Accessibility — founders and domain experts can build without a development team.
Cheap experiments — you can test whether an idea is worth building properly.
Momentum — seeing something real helps you explain your idea to customers and investors.
Security — login, permissions and database rules are easy to get subtly wrong.
Secrets — API keys can end up in code that anyone can read.
Data — personal information may be stored or exposed in ways that conflict with POPIA.
Scale — what works for ten users can slow down or fail with a thousand.
Maintenance — code nobody has read is hard to change safely, and AI fixes can introduce new bugs.

p: A prototype answers “should this exist?”. A product has to be secure, reliable and maintainable for real customers. Vibe coding is great at the first question; the second needs engineering judgement — reviews, tests, monitoring and clear ownership of the code.

list: Check who can read and change every piece of data.
Move keys and passwords into secure environment settings.
Add automated tests for the most important journeys.
Review dependencies and remove anything unused.
Set up backups, error monitoring and a way to roll back.
Document how the app works so someone else can maintain it.

sections.h: Need a second pair of eyes?
p: If you have a vibe-coded app that works but you’re not sure it’s safe to launch, our team reviews, secures and hardens AI-built code — so your prototype can become a product.

items.title: Passkeys explained: why passwords are on the way out
items.seoTitle: Passkeys Explained: How Passwordless Sign-In Works
items.description: Passkeys replace passwords with a cryptographic key stored on your device and unlocked by your fingerprint, face or PIN. How they work, why they resist phishing and what businesses should know.
items.imageAlt: A smartphone with a glowing fingerprint beside a key and an open padlock, with password dots falling away
takeaways: A passkey is a pair of cryptographic keys: a private one that stays on your device and a public one held by the website.
You unlock it with your fingerprint, face or device PIN — there’s no password to remember or steal.
Passkeys resist phishing because they only work on the genuine website they were created for.
They’re supported by major operating systems, browsers and password managers.

p: Passwords are the weakest link in online security. People reuse them, write them down and type them into convincing fake websites. Passkeys are the industry’s answer — and they’re now built into the phones and computers most of us already use.

head: Spec
In plain terms
rows: A passwordless sign-in credential based on public-key cryptography
FIDO2 and WebAuthn, developed by the FIDO Alliance and W3C
Fingerprint, face recognition or your device PIN
On your device or in your password manager — never on the website’s server
Resistant to phishing, password reuse and database leaks
Synced across devices via your platform account, plus backup sign-in options

list: When you create a passkey, your device generates two linked keys.
The public key is stored by the website; on its own it can’t be used to sign in.
The private key stays on your device or in your password manager.
To sign in, the website sends a challenge, your device signs it with the private key after you unlock it, and the website checks the signature.

p: A passkey is tied to the exact website it was created for. If a scammer builds a look-alike site, your device simply won’t offer the passkey there. And because the website never holds a secret that can be reused, a breached database doesn’t hand attackers your login.

list: Banking and fintech apps adding faster, safer sign-in.
Online stores reducing abandoned checkouts caused by forgotten passwords.
Workplace tools strengthening employee sign-in.
Customer portals and booking systems.
Offer passkeys alongside existing sign-in options during the transition.
Plan account recovery carefully — it’s where attackers will try next.
Explain the benefit in plain words on your sign-in screen.
Use well-established authentication libraries or providers rather than building your own.

p: Passkeys make signing in both easier and safer — a rare win-win in security. If you’re building a customer portal, online store or business system, it’s worth planning for them from the start.

items.title: Digital twins explained: from mines to hospitals
items.seoTitle: Digital Twins Explained: How Industries Use Virtual Models
items.description: A digital twin is a virtual model of a real asset or process, kept up to date with live data. How digital twins work and how mining, manufacturing, energy, cities and healthcare use them.
items.imageAlt: A solid model of a mining plant beside its glowing green wireframe twin, linked by streams of data
takeaways: A digital twin is a virtual copy of a real asset, system or process that updates with live data.
It lets you monitor, test changes and predict problems without touching the real thing.
Sensors, connectivity, a data platform and a model of how the asset behaves are the core ingredients.
Start with one asset and one clear question, such as “when will this pump fail?”.

p: A digital twin is a virtual model of something real — a pump, a production line, a building or an entire mine — that stays in sync with its physical counterpart through live data. Unlike a static 3D drawing, a twin changes as the real thing changes.

head: Spec
In plain terms
rows: A living virtual model of a physical asset or process
Sensors, equipment data and business systems (IoT)
Monitoring, simulation, predictive maintenance and planning
Mining, manufacturing, energy, logistics, cities and healthcare
Sensors, connectivity, data platform, model, dashboards
Collecting data without a clear decision it will improve

list: Sense — sensors measure things like temperature, vibration, pressure or location.
Connect — that data flows to a central platform in near real time.
Model — software represents how the asset behaves and how its parts relate.
Analyse — dashboards, rules and machine learning spot trends and anomalies.
Act — teams use the insights to schedule maintenance, change settings or plan improvements.
Mining — modelling processing plants, monitoring equipment health and planning ventilation and haulage.
Manufacturing — simulating production lines to remove bottlenecks before changing the real floor.
Energy and utilities — monitoring generation, grids and water networks to anticipate faults.
Cities and buildings — managing energy use, maintenance and occupancy.
Healthcare — modelling patient flow and equipment use in hospitals; research also explores twins of organs.

p: The value of a twin is the ability to ask “what if?” safely. What if we run this machine faster? What if this conveyor stops? When will this part fail? Answering those questions virtually can reduce downtime, improve safety and support better investment decisions.

list: Choose one high-value asset with a costly failure mode.
Use the data you already have before adding new sensors.
Define the decision the twin should improve, and how you’ll measure success.
Build a simple dashboard first; add simulation and prediction later.

p: Digital twins rely on data pipelines, dashboards and integrations — the same building blocks as our AI & Data Engineering and Business Systems work. We can help you turn existing data into a practical first view of your operation.

why.body: Design, motion, frontend, backend and AI engineering in one team of three, and the people you speak to are the people doing the work.

team.title: Three people. One studio.
team.intro: Design, motion and engineering under one roof. The people you speak to are the people doing the work — no hand-offs to strangers.

members.name: Lulamile Mkhungela
bio: Lulamile founded LulaZel Digital Studio in 2019 to bring design and development together. He leads every project from the first conversation to launch — shaping the strategy, designing the journeys and interfaces, and building the frontend that customers actually use.
His focus is simple: turn a business problem into something clear, useful and ready for the real world.

members.name: Ronald Modiba
bio: Ronald brings brands and ideas to life through graphic design, motion and animation. A multimedia graduate of Tshwane University of Technology, he has spent more than four years turning storyboards into animated videos, infographics and interactive digital learning, using Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop and After Effects, Vyond, and 3D tools such as 3ds Max and Unity.
He and Lulamile first worked together at The Digital Academy. At LulaZel he leads brand visuals, motion graphics and animated explainers.

members.name: Keitumetse Donald Bokaba
bio: Keitumetse is a certified AI engineer and backend developer: Microsoft-certified, with three Azure certifications and hands-on machine-learning and generative-AI experience on AWS. With a background in data science and software development, he builds the systems behind the screen — databases, APIs, cloud infrastructure and the AI features that run on them.

He and Lulamile were on the winning team at Empire Partner Foundation’s 2021 GBV hackathon, where they built HashScape, a mobile app that uses AI to help identify signs of abuse. At LulaZel he leads backend and AI engineering.
